name: Design a Distributed Message Queue
intent: Build the broker behind a Kafka-style log: topics split into replicated, append-only partitions that take millions of messages per second, keep order where it matters, and let many consumer groups read at their own pace.
codeTitle: a partitioned, replicated log with committed offsets
finalIntro: One message from a producer to a replicated partition and on to a consumer group.
prompt: Design the message broker itself, not an application that uses one. Producers write records to named topics, and consumers read them later, possibly many times and by several independent applications. It must take hundreds of thousands of messages per second, keep the order of messages for the same key, survive the loss of a machine without losing acknowledged messages, and let a group of consumers share the work of one topic.
functional: Producers append records to a topic, optionally with a key
Consumers read a topic in order, from any position, and can replay old records
Consumers in the same group share the topic's work, and different groups each get every record
A group remembers how far it has read, and continues from there after a restart
Records are kept for a configured time or size, not deleted when read
Topics can be created, and given more partitions, while the system runs
nonFunctional: Hundreds of thousands of writes per second on a modest cluster, at a few milliseconds each
Messages with the same key are read in the order they were written
A message acknowledged with the strongest setting survives the loss of any one machine
A broker failure does not stop the topic for more than a few seconds
A slow consumer must not slow producers or other consumers
The producer chooses between speed and safety for each write

firstAttempt.text: One server holds an in-memory queue per topic. Producers push messages onto it, the server gives each message to one waiting consumer, and deletes the message when that consumer acknowledges it. A database table can stand in for the memory if the queue must survive restarts.
limits: Deleting on acknowledgement means a message can be read only once, so a second application, a bug fix or a new feature cannot replay history
Tracking and deleting each message individually is random work on disk, which caps throughput at far below the target
One server holds every topic, so its memory, disk and network are the ceiling, and its failure stops everything
If the server dies, queued messages are lost or stranded on its disk
There is no useful order once several consumers take messages in parallel

steps.title: Keep messages in an append-only log, and let readers track their own position
steps.problem: A queue that deletes each message when it is read can be read only once, and the random bookkeeping of removing individual messages is slow.
steps.fix: Store a topic's messages as a log: new records are only ever added at the end, and each gets the next number, its offset. The log is cut into segment files of, say, 1 GB. Only the newest segment is written, so every write is sequential, which disks and the operating system do very fast. A sparse index per segment maps some offsets to file positions, so reading from any offset is one lookup and then a sequential scan. Nothing is deleted when it is read. A consumer simply remembers the offset it has reached, and it can rewind to replay. Reads of recent data come from the operating system's page cache, and the bytes can go from cache to network without being copied through the application.
steps.tradeoff: Writes and reads are sequential and cheap, many readers cost almost nothing, and replay is free. The broker cannot reorder, skip or remove one message, a consumer must keep its own position, and old data only goes away by deleting whole segments.

steps.title: Split a topic into partitions, and choose the partition by key
steps.problem: One log lives on one machine, and one machine cannot take the writes or serve the reads for a whole company.
steps.fix: A topic is divided into partitions, each its own log, spread over the brokers. A producer picks the partition for every record: when the record has a key, it takes a stable hash of the key modulo the number of partitions, so all records of one key land in the same partition. Without a key it spreads records over partitions in batches. Order is guaranteed only inside a partition, which is enough when the order that matters is per key, such as per account or per device. Consumers are assigned whole partitions, which gives parallelism up to the partition count.
steps.tradeoff: Throughput grows with the number of partitions, and per-key order is kept. There is no order across partitions, a very hot key makes a hot partition, and adding partitions later changes the key-to-partition mapping, so records of one key can then be split across the old and the new placement.

steps.title: Replicate every partition: a leader, followers and an in-sync set
steps.problem: A partition on one broker is lost when that broker's disk is, and the topic stops while the broker is down.
steps.fix: Each partition is stored on, say, 3 brokers. One is the leader and takes all reads and writes. The others are followers that fetch from the leader like any consumer and append to their own copy. The in-sync replicas (ISR) are the leader plus the followers that are keeping up. The high watermark is the highest offset that every in-sync replica has, and consumers only see records up to it. The producer picks an acknowledgement level: 0 returns immediately, 1 returns when the leader has written, all returns when every in-sync replica has it. A minimum in-sync count refuses writes when too few replicas are in sync. When a leader dies, a new one is chosen from the in-sync replicas, and that choice is why acknowledged records survive.
steps.tradeoff: With acks=all and 3 replicas, a record that was acknowledged survives the loss of any one broker. It costs an extra round trip to the followers for every write, and a slow follower is dropped from the in-sync set so that it does not hold everyone back. With acks=1 a failure can lose records that were acknowledged, and acks=0 can lose them without the producer ever knowing.

steps.title: Share a topic's work with consumer groups and committed offsets
steps.problem: Several consumers should split the work of one topic, each application should see every record, and a restarted consumer must find where it left off.
steps.fix: Consumers join a named group. A group coordinator, which is a broker, gives each partition to exactly one member of the group, so each record is processed by one member of each group, and different groups read independently. Consumers pull records in batches from the leader, which lets a slow consumer fall behind without affecting anyone else. A group records its progress by committing offsets into an internal compacted topic. When a member joins, leaves or stops sending heartbeats, the group rebalances and the partitions are redistributed. The new owner continues from the last committed offset.
steps.tradeoff: Work is shared, and every group has its own view of the same data. Where the commit goes decides the failure mode: committing after processing may repeat messages after a crash (at least once), and committing before may skip them (at most once). Rebalances pause consumption, and a consumer that is too slow to poll is removed from the group, which causes yet another rebalance.

steps.title: Expire old segments, compact by key, and move cold data away
steps.problem: A log that only grows will fill every disk, but readers need history for replay and for slow consumers.
steps.fix: Retention is applied to whole segments, by age or by total size: when every record in an old segment is past the limit, the file is deleted, which is cheap. A topic that holds the latest value for each key, such as the committed-offsets topic, can use compaction instead, where a background cleaner rewrites segments to keep only the newest record for each key. Cold segments can be moved to cheaper object storage and read from there, so retention can be long while brokers keep only the recent part on local disks.
steps.tradeoff: Disk use is bounded and predictable, and compaction gives a table-like topic. A consumer that falls behind by more than the retention loses the records it had not read. Deleting by segment means records live somewhat longer than the limit, and reads from cold storage are slower.

steps.title: Run a controller quorum, and make producers safe to retry
steps.problem: Someone has to decide which broker leads which partition and who is in sync, and a producer that retries after a lost acknowledgement writes the record twice.
steps.fix: A small group of controller nodes agrees on the cluster's metadata, which is the topics, the partitions, each leader and each in-sync set, using a consensus log. When a broker fails, the controller picks new leaders from the in-sync replicas, and clients refresh their cached metadata. Producers are made idempotent: each has an id and numbers its records per partition, so the leader recognises a retried record by its sequence number and drops it. Transactions on top of this write to several partitions atomically. The cluster is watched by metrics such as under-replicated partitions and consumer lag.
steps.tradeoff: Failover takes seconds, retries cannot create duplicates inside the log, and the cluster is observable. A controller quorum is more to operate, a transaction costs extra coordination, and exactly-once is only true for the data inside the log: an effect on an outside system still needs an idempotent consumer.

failures.scenario: A partition leader's machine dies in the middle of writes
failures.impact: Writes to its partitions fail for a moment. With acks=1 or acks=0, records that the leader had acknowledged but its followers had not yet copied are lost.
failures.answer: The controller picks a new leader from the in-sync replicas, and producers refresh their metadata and retry. With acks=all, every acknowledged record was already on all in-sync replicas, so none are lost. Retried records are dropped by sequence number when the producer is idempotent. The old leader truncates its log to the new leader's when it returns.

failures.scenario: A follower falls behind and leaves the in-sync set
failures.impact: If replicas = 3 but only the leader is in sync, acks=all is as weak as acks=1, and a leader failure now loses data.
failures.answer: Set the minimum in-sync replicas to 2, so that the partition refuses writes when fewer than two replicas are in sync. Producers get an error and retry, which trades availability for safety. Alerts on under-replicated partitions bring the slow broker to a person quickly.

failures.scenario: A consumer takes too long to process a batch and is removed from the group
failures.impact: The group rebalances, its partitions move, and the batch it was working on is processed again by the new owner. If it keeps happening, the group rebalances over and over.
failures.answer: Keep processing time per poll well below the poll timeout by taking smaller batches, and send heartbeats from a separate thread. Make processing idempotent, because repeats are normal, and commit after processing. Cooperative rebalancing moves only the partitions that need to move.

failures.scenario: One key is far hotter than the others
failures.impact: All of its records hash to one partition, so one leader and one consumer are overloaded while the rest are idle.
failures.answer: Make the key finer if the order only has to hold for something smaller, such as the order and not the whole customer. For the few keys that remain hot, add a salt to the key and merge afterwards, accepting that order within that key is lost. Watching the per-partition rates shows the problem early.

failures.scenario: A consumer is down for longer than the retention period
failures.impact: The offset it committed no longer exists, because the segments were deleted, and it cannot continue from where it stopped.
failures.answer: The consumer gets an out-of-range error and must restart from the earliest available record or the latest, by configuration, and rebuild its state from a snapshot if it needs one. Alert on consumer lag well before it nears the retention limit, and keep retention longer than the longest outage the consumers should survive.

alternatives.title: How much the producer waits for

options.name: acks=0
options.pro: Lowest latency and the highest throughput, since nothing is awaited
options.con: Failures lose records silently, and the producer cannot know

options.name: acks=1
options.pro: A leader write is fast, and most failures lose nothing
options.con: A leader that dies before its followers copy a record loses an acknowledged record

options.name: acks=all with a minimum in-sync of 2
options.pro: An acknowledged record survives the loss of any one broker
options.con: Slower by a follower round trip, and writes are refused when too few replicas are in sync

alternatives.pick: acks=all with at least 2 in-sync replicas for data that matters, acks=1 for metrics and logs that can lose a few records.

alternatives.title: How consumption is tracked

options.name: A log with committed offsets per group
options.pro: Replay, many independent groups, and cheap sequential storage
options.con: No per-message acknowledgement, retry or delay, and order is only per partition

options.name: A queue that deletes on acknowledgement
options.pro: Per-message acknowledgement, retries, dead-letter queues and priorities are natural
options.con: No replay, and reading the same data again for a second application needs a copy

alternatives.pick: The log for streams that several applications read or replay, and a classic queue for work items that need individual acknowledgement.

alternatives.title: How records are assigned to partitions

options.name: Hash of the key
options.pro: Per-key order and local state in the consumer
options.con: Hot keys, and a changed partition count remaps keys

options.name: Round robin in batches
options.pro: Perfectly even load and the best batching

options.name: A custom rule
options.pro: Can keep related data together or spread known hot keys
options.con: Producers and consumers must agree on a rule that is easy to get wrong

alternatives.pick: The key hash when order matters, and round robin when it does not.

alternatives.title: Who holds the cluster metadata

options.name: A separate coordination service
options.pro: A proven system, with a long history
options.con: Another cluster to run, and metadata that has to be synchronised with it

options.name: A controller quorum built into the brokers
options.pro: One system to operate, and fast failover with a large partition count
options.con: The consensus protocol is part of the broker, so it must be correct and well tested

alternatives.pick: A built-in controller quorum running a consensus log.
